hook.text: The Penrose triangle looks like a solid 3D object on paper—until you trace its edges and find they can't connect.

buildup.text: Impossible figures exploit local consistency: each corner looks correct, but the global structure contradicts itself.

discovery.text: Your brain processes depth cues locally, not globally. It accepts each junction before noticing the whole is impossible.

twist.text: M.C. Escher built entire worlds from these contradictions—staircases that climb forever, water that flows uphill.

climax.text: Impossible figures reveal that 3D perception is assembled from local rules, not a unified spatial model.

punchline.text: Your brain builds depth one corner at a time.

quiz.question: Why do impossible figures look plausible at first?
options: The brain processes depth cues locally

details.summary: Impossible figures like the Penrose triangle and Escher's staircases look coherent locally but cannot exist as three-dimensional objects. Your brain processes each corner correctly but cannot integrate them into a consistent whole, creating a fascinating perceptual contradiction.
details.whyItMatters: Impossible figures reveal how the brain processes parts of a scene locally before attempting global integration, and what happens when integration fails.
takeaways: Each part of an impossible figure looks correct in isolation
The brain cannot integrate all parts into a consistent 3D shape
They reveal local-before-global processing in visual perception

faq.question: Why do impossible figures look convincing at first glance?
faq.answer: Your brain processes local regions first and each corner or junction follows valid 3D geometry rules. The impossibility only emerges when you trace the entire figure and find the pieces cannot connect consistently. Initial perception succeeds locally but fails globally.

faq.question: Can impossible figures exist in physical form?
faq.answer: Only from one specific viewpoint. Sculptors create objects that look like impossible figures from a single angle by using carefully designed gaps and angles that are invisible from that position. Move the viewer and the illusion breaks immediately.
